topic.name: The Nth Term of a Geometric Sequence

question.text: Find the formula for the $n$th term of the following geometric sequence. \[ 1, \: \dfrac 3 2, \: \dfrac 9 4, \: \ldots \]
question.explanation:
The first term of the sequence is $a_1=1$ and the second term is $a_2=\dfrac 3 2,$ so we can find the common ratio, as follows:

\begin{align*} r &= \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)}{1} = \dfrac{3}{2} \end{align*}

Now that we know the common ratio is $r=\dfrac{3}{2},$ we can complete the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= 1 \cdot \left( \dfrac 3 2 \right) ^ {n - 1} \\[5pt] &= \left( \dfrac 3 2 \right) ^ {n - 1} \end{align*}

example.title: Finding a Formula for the Nth Term of a Geometric Sequence

question.text: Find the formula for the $n$th term of a sequence if the $4$th term is $-135$ and the common ratio is $-3.$
question.explanation:
The common ratio is $r=-3,$ so we can start writing the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= a_1 \cdot (-3)^{n-1} \end{align*}

However, we still need to figure out the first term $a_1.$ We know that the $4$th term is $a_4=-135,$ so we can solve for the first term as follows:

\begin{align*} a_4 &= a_1 \cdot (-3)^{4-1} \\[5pt] -135 &= a_1 \cdot (-3)^3 \\[5pt] -135 &= a_1 \cdot (-27) \\[5pt] 5 &= a_1 \end{align*}

Now that we know the first term is $a_1=5,$ we can complete the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot 5^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{5 (-3)^{n-1} }\\[3pt] \end{align*}

question.text: If the fifth term of a geometric sequence is $\dfrac{1}{8}$ and the common ratio is $\dfrac{1}{4},$ then the eighth term of this sequence is
question.explanation:
The common ratio is $r=\dfrac{1}{4},$ so we can start writing the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= a_1 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{n-1} \end{align*}

However, we still need to figure out the first term $a_1.$ We know that the $5$th term is $a_5=\dfrac{1}{8},$ so we can solve for the first term as follows:

\begin{align*} a_5 &= a_1 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{5-1} \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{8} &= a_1 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^4 \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{8} &= a_1 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{256}\right) \\[5pt] \dfrac{256}{8} &= a_1 \\[5pt] 32 &= a_1 \end{align*}

Now that we know the first term is $a_1=32,$ we can complete the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

\begin{align*} a_n &= a_1 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= 32 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{n-1} \end{align*}

Then, we can use this formula to compute the $8$th term:

\begin{align*} a_{8} &= 32 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{8-1} \\[5pt] &= 32 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^7 \\[5pt] &= 2^5\cdot \dfrac{1}{4^7} \\[5pt] %&= \dfrac{32}{4^7}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2^5}{(2^2)^7}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2^5}{2^{14}}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2^9} \end{align*}

Therefore, the $8$th term is $a_{8} = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{2^9}}.$
